text: The Rust scheduler in doeff: one scheduler, with two implementations.
In doeff, concurrency is effects too. The program yields Spawn and Gather, and scheduled is the handler that answers them, resuming k with each answer.
That handler comes in Rust and in Python, with the same meaning. Rust is the default; Python is opt-in.
Which one runs? The argument decides first, then the environment variable DOEFF SCHEDULER, then the default.
The default is rust. Any other name is refused with a ValueError.
Same meaning: here is one program, run under both implementations.
Tasks a and b wait on one promise, and task b has high priority. Task slow waits on a promise that is never kept.
The opener keeps the promise. Task b wakes first, then task a, in both implementations.
Cancel unwinds task slow: its finally block runs, and then Wait raises TaskCancelledError.
The same result, the same order, and the same sixty-four trace events.
What moved to Rust is every decision the scheduler makes for an effect: task state, the ready queue, Cancel, and deadlock detection.
What stays in Python is every class your code sees, raises, or subclasses, along with the warnings, the trace, and the step limit.
So under both, a subclass of an effect resolves as its parent, and Spawn still gives back a Python Task.
And it is faster. Here is the page's benchmark, run again: microseconds of CPU time per operation.
Wherever the scheduler does the work, Rust takes six to twelve times less CPU time.
An effect that only passes through gains least, because its time is spent outside the scheduler.
The Rust scheduler: the same effects, the same handler, the same meaning, in a fraction of the time.
